Bhima is dearest to you of all your brothers, bull of the Bharatas; why do you not go to him now that he is in difficulty?
mahabharata:10:12.4	That weapon named Brahmashira which Drona, conqueror of enemy cities, told his son, which could burn even the earth,
mahabharata:10:12.5	that great and greatly fortunate teacher, the banner of all bowmen, gave to Dhananjaya, being pleased with him.
mahabharata:10:12.6	His son, intolerant, asked him for it in the same way; then he gave it to his son, not very gladly.
mahabharata:10:12.7	The teacher, knower of all dharma, knew the fickleness of his great-souled son, and did not ever seek his son out.
mahabharata:10:12.8	'Even in the utmost calamity, dear one, you must not use this weapon in battle, especially against men.'
mahabharata:10:12.9	So said the teacher Drona to his son; and afterwards he said, 'You, bull among men, will never stay on the path of the good.'
[Ashvatthaman said:] "That fierce austerity which, truly valiant, my father (Drona) practised, the teacher of the Bharatas received from Agastya,
the weapon named Brahmashira, honoured by gods and Gandharvas; that is now in me, Dasharha, as it was in my father.
Taking that weapon from us, best of the Yadus, give me too the discus that destroys foes in battle.'
[Krishna said:] "Then, O king, he, with joined palms, I being pleased, begged earnestly from me the weapon, bull of the Bharatas.
'Gods, Danavas, Gandharvas, men, birds and serpents all together are not equal to a hundredth part of my might.
This bow, this spear, this discus, this mace—whichever weapon you wish, I shall give you from me.
Take whatever you can raise or use in battle, without the weapon you wish me to give you.'
He chose the iron discus, with its fine nave, a thousand spokes and a thunderbolt hub, mighty-armed one, vying with me.
Told by me, 'Take the discus,' he approached and suddenly seized it with his left hand, but he could not move it from its place, Achyuta.
Then he tried to take it with the right hand also; trying with all his effort, he still could not manage it.
Then even with all his strength he could neither lift nor move it; Drona's son, very dejected, having made supreme effort, weary, turned away, Bharata.
When he, bewildered by his aim, turned back from it, I spoke to Ashvatthaman, taking leave affectionately:
'He who among gods and men has reached the highest standard, the wielder of Gandiva, white-horsed, with the best of apes as banner,
who in a duel conquered and pleased in person the god of gods, blue-throated Shankara, lord of Uma,
than whom no other man on earth is dearer to me, to whom I would give anything, my wives and my sons,
even by that friend, Brahmana, Partha of untroubled deeds, was this never said which you say to me.
I, having practised great, dreadful celibacy for twelve years and gone to the side of the Himalaya, worshipped him with austerity,
and there was born to Rukmini, who kept the same vow, Sanatkumara the radiant, my son named Pradyumna.
Even he never asked for this great divine, incomparable discus of mine, fool, which you have asked for.
Mighty Rama never said such a thing, nor Gada, nor Samba, which you have asked for.
Nor have other great chariot-warriors of the Vrishnis and Andhakas dwelling in Dvaraka ever said what you have asked.
Honoured by all the Yadavas as the teacher of the Bharatas' son, best of chariot-warriors, why do you wish to fight with the discus, dear one?'
Thus addressed by me, Drona's son replied to me: 'Having honoured you, Krishna, I wished to fight with you.
I asked for the discus, honoured by gods and Danavas, so as to be invincible; this I tell you truly, lord.
Without obtaining this hard-to-obtain wish from you, Keshava, I shall return, Govinda; bid me farewell kindly.
This discus with the fine nave, held by you, bull of the Vrishnis, the one without equal, no other on earth can approach.'
Having said this much, Drona's son took from me a pair of horses, wealth and various jewels, and went away, the boy.
He is hasty, wicked, fickle and cruel, and he knows the Brahmashira weapon; therefore Vrikodara must be protected."
The army of Sugriva drew the right side of the chariot, bright as the sunrise, and on the left the two at the rear, Meghapushpa and Balahaka, drew.
A divine banner-staff, made by Vishvakarma and adorned with many jewels, appeared on the chariot as if a raised illusion.
On it stood the son of Vinata (Garuda), radiant with a halo of rays; the banner of that truthful one, enemy of serpents, was seen.
Hrishikesha, the banner of all bowmen, mounted behind, with Arjuna and Yudhishthira, king of the Kurus, of true deeds.
The two great souls shone standing on either side of Dasharha, bearer of the Sharnga bow, on the chariot, like the Ashvins with Vasava.
Putting them on the chariot honoured by the worlds, Dasharha urged the excellent horses, swift as a goad, to speed.
The horses suddenly sprang up, carrying the excellent chariot on which the two Pandavas and the bull of the Yadus stood.
As the swift horses bore the bearer of Sharnga, a great sound arose like the flight of birds.
The great chariot-warriors, though they met him, could not restrain the son of Kunti, blazing with anger and intent on his enemy.
While those glorious firm archers watched, he went with his speeding horses to the bank of the Bhagirathi, where it was heard that Drona's son, slayer of the sons of the great souls, was.
He saw the great, renowned Krishna Dvaipayana Vyasa seated at the water's edge with sages.
And he saw close by that cruel-deeded Drona's son, smeared with ghee, wearing kusha-grass bark, his hair-ends dusty.
The son of Kunti, mighty-armed Bhimasena, rushed at him with his bow and arrow ready and said, "Stand, stand!"
Seeing him of the terrible bow with bow raised, and the two brothers standing behind on Janardana's chariot, Drona's son was distressed and thought the end had come.
Undaunted, he thought of that divine supreme weapon and took a reed with his left hand; reaching that calamity, he invoked the Brahma weapon.
Not bearing those heroes standing with divine weapons, he cried out in rage a dreadful word, "For the Pandavas to be no more!"
Having said this, tiger among kings, mighty Drona's son released that weapon for the bewilderment of all worlds.
Then from that reed a fire arose, as if about to burn the three worlds, like Time, the Ender, Yama.
[Krishna said:] "Arjuna, Arjuna, the divine weapon that is in your heart, taught by Drona—its time has now come, Pandava.
For the protection of your brothers and yourself, Bharata, you too release in battle the weapon that stops weapons."
Thus addressed by Keshava, the Pandava, slayer of heroes, quickly descended from his chariot with his bow and arrow.
First saying "Peace" to the teacher's son, then to himself, and to all his brothers, the scorcher of foes,
bowing to the gods and to all his teachers, thinking of the auspicious, he released the weapon, saying "Let weapon be quelled by weapon."
Then that weapon, suddenly released by the wielder of Gandiva, blazed with great flames, like the fire at the end of an age.
Likewise the weapon of fierce-splendoured Drona's son blazed with great flame, enveloped in an orb of radiance.
Thunderclaps were many, meteors fell by thousands, and great fear arose in all beings.
Narada, and the righteous Grandsire of the Bharatas (Vyasa), both came to pacify the two heroes, the son of Bharadvaja and Dhananjaya.
Those two sages, knowers of all dharma, well-wishers of all beings, of supreme splendour, stood between the two blazing weapons.
Approaching between them, unassailable, the renowned best of sages stood there like two blazing fires.
Unassailable by living beings, honoured by gods and Danavas, they came to quell the energy of the weapons, wishing the good of the worlds.
[The sages said:] "The great chariot-warriors of old who knew various weapons, and who are past—this weapon was never used by them against men."
[Vyasa said:] The best of speakers, with joined palms, said to those two sages then: "I used the weapon so that weapon might be quelled by weapon.
When this supreme weapon is withdrawn, the sinful Drona's son will surely burn us all entirely by the energy of his weapon.
In this matter, what is beneficial to us and the worlds in every way, you two, like gods, ought to withdraw it."
Having said this, Dhananjaya withdrew the weapon again; its withdrawal is hard in battle even for the gods.
Once released in battle, none but the Pandava could withdraw that supreme weapon, not even Shatakratu in person.
For it is born of Brahma's energy; released by an unrefined one, it cannot be recalled except by one in the vow of celibacy.
One who has not practised celibacy and who, having released it, recalls it, has that weapon cut off the head of him and his kin.
Arjuna, a celibate and vow-keeper, who had gained that hard-to-gain weapon, though afflicted by the utmost calamity, did not release the weapon."
Unable to withdraw the supreme weapon in battle, Drona's son, dejected, said to Dvaipayana, O king:

It was said by me, afflicted by calamity and wishing to save my life: this weapon was released from fear of Bhimasena, sage.
mahabharata:10:15.14	And unrighteousness was done by Bhimasena in the battle, who, wishing to slay Dhritarashtra's son, fought deceitfully, revered one.
mahabharata:10:15.15	Therefore, Brahmana, this weapon was released by me, unrefined; I cannot withdraw it now.
mahabharata:10:15.16	This divine weapon, hard to approach, was released by me, sage, having consecrated it with fire's energy with the words 'for the Pandavas to be no more.'
mahabharata:10:15.17	It is aimed at the end of the Pandavas, and today will deprive all the sons of Pandu of life.
mahabharata:10:15.18	This sin was done, Brahmana, by me with a mind seized by anger, releasing the weapon in battle wishing the slaying of the Parthas.
[Vyasa said:] "Dear one, the learned Partha Dhananjaya knew the Brahmashira weapon, yet did not release it in anger or for slaying you in the fight.
Arjuna released it in battle to quell your weapon with weapon, and he withdrew it again.
Though he obtained the Brahma weapon by your father's instruction, the mighty-armed Dhananjaya did not waver from kshatriya dharma.
Why do you wish to slay such a steadfast, good man, knower of all weapons, with his brothers and kin?
Where the Brahmashira weapon is met by the supreme weapon, the rain-god does not rain on that kingdom for twelve years.
For this reason the mighty-armed Pandava, though capable, does not strike down your weapon, wishing the welfare of his subjects.
The Pandavas, you and the kingdom must always be protected by us; therefore withdraw this divine weapon, mighty-armed one.
Let there be freedom from anger in you, and let the Parthas be free of harm; the royal sage Pandava does not wish to conquer by unrighteousness.
And give them the jewel that is on your head; taking it, the Pandavas will give you back your life."
[Drona's son said:] "Of the jewels obtained by the Pandavas and the wealth obtained by the Kauravas, this jewel of mine is superior to them,
by wearing which there is no fear from weapons, disease or hunger, nor from gods, Danavas or serpents in any way,
nor fear of hosts of Rakshasas or of thieves; of such power is this jewel; I may not give it up in any way.
But what the revered one says I must do next: this jewel is here, and I am here; this reed will fall upon the wombs of the Pandavas, unfailing as it has been raised."
[Vyasa said:] "Do so, and let no other thought ever be yours; release this on the wombs of the Pandavas and desist."
[Vaishampayana said:] Then, greatly distressed, Ashvatthaman, hearing Dvaipayana's words, released that supreme weapon on the wombs.
Seeing the daughter of Virata, the daughter-in-law of the wielder of Gandiva, who had gone to Upaplavya, a Brahmana who kept a vow said earlier:
When the Kurus are exhausted, your son will be born; for this reason he, while in the womb, will be called Parikshit.
The word of that good man will surely come true: a son named Parikshit will be born, continuing their line again.
Thus Govinda, best of the Satvatas, spoke, and Drona's son, greatly enraged, then replied:

It is not as you say through partiality, Keshava, lotus-eyed; my word will not be otherwise.
mahabharata:10:16.7	This weapon raised by me will fall on the womb of the daughter of Virata, whom you wish to protect.
[Vasudeva said:] "The fall of the supreme weapon will be unfailing, but that embryo, born dead, will gain long life.
But all the wise know you as a coward, a sinner, repeatedly a doer of sin, killer of children.
Knowing the supreme weapons, established in the vow of kshatriya dharma, the righteous one will rule the earth for sixty years.
Hereafter, the mighty-armed king of the Kurus, a king named Parikshit, will be born, ill-minded one, before your eyes; behold the power of my austerity and of truth, vilest of men."
[Vyasa said:] "Because you have done this dreadful deed to us, disregarding us, and because such is your conduct for a Brahmana though good,
therefore what the son of Devaki has said, supreme words, will surely befall you, petty-deeded one; go away from here."
[Ashvatthaman said:] "I shall stay among men with you, Brahmana; let the revered one and this best of men be truthful."
[Vaishampayana said:] Giving his jewel to the great-souled Pandavas, Drona's son, dejected, went to the forest in the sight of them all.
And the Pandavas, their foes slain, putting Govinda, Krishna Dvaipayana and the great sage Narada before them,
took the jewel born with Drona's son and hastened to Draupadi, who was fasting to death, the high-minded.
Then those tigers among men, with fine horses swift as the wind, with Dasharha returned again to the camp.
Descending hastily from their chariots, the great chariot-warriors saw Draupadi Krishna in distress, themselves in greater distress.
Approaching her, joyless, afflicted with grief and sorrow, the Pandavas with Keshava stood surrounding her.
Then, permitted by the king, mighty Bhimasena gave the divine jewel and said these words:

This is your jewel, auspicious one; the slayer of your sons is conquered; rise, cast off grief and remember kshatriya dharma.
mahabharata:10:16.27	Remember, timid one, the words you spoke, dark-eyed, to Vasudeva, slayer of Madhu, when he went to make peace:
mahabharata:10:16.28	'I have no husbands, no sons, no brothers, and you, Govinda, have none, if the king desires peace.'
mahabharata:10:16.29	You spoke dreadful words to the best of men, befitting kshatriya dharma; you ought to remember them.
mahabharata:10:16.30	Duryodhana the sinner, obstructor of the kingdom, is slain, and Duhshasana's blood was drunk by me as he writhed.
mahabharata:10:16.31	We are quit of our debt of enmity, and no one need speak of it; Drona's son was conquered and released, out of respect for his Brahmanhood.
mahabharata:10:16.32	His fame has been brought down, lady, and his body only is left; he has been parted from the jewel and has laid his weapon on the ground.
[Draupadi said:] "I have become quit of the debt entirely; my teacher's son is my teacher; let the king wear this jewel on his head, Bharata."
[Vaishampayana said:] Taking it, the king then placed it on his head, saying "It is the teacher's leavings," also by Draupadi's word.
Then, bearing the excellent divine jewel on his head, the lord, the great king, shone like a mountain with the moon.
Then Krishna, high-minded, afflicted with grief for her sons, rose up, and the king of dharma questioned mighty-armed Krishna.

How, Krishna, were all my sons, great chariot-warriors, slain by the sinful, petty Drona's son of impure deeds?
mahabharata:10:17.3	And the sons of Drupada, skilled in weapons, valiant, fighting hundreds of thousands, were felled by Drona's son.
mahabharata:10:17.4	He to whom the great archer Drona did not show his back in battle, the best of chariot-warriors Dhrishtadyumna—how did he slay him?
mahabharata:10:17.5	What deed of such sort did the teacher's son do, bull among men, that alone he slew the whole of our camp?
[Vasudeva said:] "Surely Drona's son took refuge alone with the imperishable lord of the lords of gods, and so he slew many.
For Mahadeva, when pleased, would give even immortality, and Girisha would give the strength by which one could strike down even Indra.
I know Mahadeva in truth, bull of the Bharatas, and his many ancient deeds.
He is the beginning, the middle and the end of beings, Bharata; this whole world moves by his action.
Seeing Girisha broken in the water, he said to his father: 'If I have no elder than you, then I shall protect the creatures.'
His father said to him: 'There is no man elder than you; this Sthanu lies sunk in the water; do your work confidently.'
He created the seven beings and the Prajapatis beginning with Daksha, by whom he made this whole fourfold host of beings.
Those created beings, hungry, all, as soon as created, wishing to devour the Prajapati, suddenly ran at him, O king.
Being devoured, seeking protection, he ran to the Grandsire: 'May the revered one protect me from these; let their livelihood be ordained.'
Then he gave them food: herbs, plants, and moving beings, the weak for the strong.
Those creatures, their food provided, went away contented as they had come, and then grew, O king, delighted, in their own wombs.
When the host of beings had grown, and the teacher of the world was pleased, the eldest rose from the water and saw these creatures.
Seeing the creatures of many forms, grown by their own energy, the revered Rudra grew angry and tore off his own organ.
Cast down, it stood upright on the earth; the imperishable Brahma said to him with words that seemed to soothe:
'What have you done, Sharva, staying so long in the water? Why have you torn out your organ and thrown it on the earth?'
Then he, filled with rage, said to the teacher of the world: 'These creatures were created by another; what shall I do with this?
Food obtained by austerity for the creatures, grandsire, the herbs, will go on returning as the creatures go on forever.'
Having said this, enraged, Bhava went dejected to the foot of the Munjavat mountain to practise austerity, the great ascetic.
Then, undisturbed, they arranged places fit for sacrifice, the gods who were entitled to shares, and the sacrificial materials.
Not knowing Rudra truly, those gods did not appoint a share for the god Sthanu, O king.
When his share was not appointed, the hide-clad one, seeking his share by force at the sacrifice, first created a bow.
The sacrifice of the world, the sacrifice of action, the household sacrifice eternal, the sacrifice made of the five elements, and the fifth, the sacrifice of men.
The matted-haired one, wishing for sacrifice, fashioned the bow with the world-sacrifice; the bow that was created measured five cubits.
The vashatkara was its string, Bharata, and four limbs of the sacrifice were in its construction.
Then the angered Mahadeva, taking that bow, came to the place where the gods were sacrificing.
Seeing that unfallen celibate with bow in hand, the goddess Earth was troubled and the mountains shook.
Then he pierced the sacrifice in the heart with a terrible arrow; the sacrifice fled, becoming a deer, with the fire.
In that same form it reached heaven and shone, pursued by Rudra, Yudhishthira, in the sky.
When the sacrifice had fled, no consciousness came to the gods; the gods lost their senses and nothing was known.
Tryambaka, enraged, broke with the tip of his bow the arms of Savitri, the eyes of Bhaga and the teeth of Pushan.
Then the gods and all the limbs of the sacrifice fled in every direction; some reeled there as though lifeless.
Having scattered them all, the blue-throated one laughed and, planting the tip of his bow, stopped the gods.
Then the gods spoke; the string of his bow was cut, and that bow, with its string cut, suddenly, O king, quivered.
Then the gods, the bow unstrung, went to the best of gods for refuge, with the sacrifice, and the lord showed grace.
Then, pleased, the revered one cast his anger into the water; becoming fire, it dries up the water ever, lord.
He gave back the eyes of Bhaga, the arms of Savitri, the teeth of Pushan and the sacrifice, Pandava.
Then all this was well again, and the gods assigned him a share of all the oblations.
When he was angry, the whole world was ill at ease, lord; when he was pleased again it was well; that valiant one is pleased with him.
Then, all your sons, great chariot-warriors, were slain, and many other heroes and the Panchalas with their followers."
Time has no favourite and no enemy, best of the Kurus, nor is it neutral anywhere; Time draws everything along.
Bhimasena's strength, Phalguna's skill, your wisdom, O king of kings, and the twins' modesty,
All the activities in the world and likewise the withdrawals, and all their modifications, are said to have Time as their nature.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Without doubt the horse sacrifice would purify even the earth; but I have a certain purpose, and you ought to hear it here."
Bhima too followed, sighing, the king (Yudhishthira), son of Dharma, but looking at Dhritarashtra was ever ill at ease.
The men proclaimed there by Keshava's command: "A pilgrimage to the sea is to be made by you, bulls among men."
[Vaishampayana said:] Having said this, the king, son of Dharma, without looking back at her, went on, the righteous, wise bull among men, composing his mind.
The son of Kunti also saw a kuta-shalmali tree, hard to touch, with sharp thorns, and the tortures of sinners.
